articles.title: The RTX 5090’s 16-pin connector just got a free pin-by-pin watchdog
articles.summary: A developer known as Codeh4ck released a free, open-source Windows app , RTX Lens, to help assuage melting power connector fears for owners of powerful RTX 5080 and 5090 GPUs. The app can read per-pin current information on Asus Astral cards, the WireView Pro II GPU monitoring device from Thermal Grizzly, and MSI MPG Ai1300TS/Ai1600TS PSUs, enabling an optional shutdown for persistent warnings. It works by reading current at the GPU, PSU, or both ends of the cable, and can even notify you by phone to provide extra protection for your investment. The project’s README says that the app allows reading of “GPU power, pin currents, and temperatures at a glance.” The per-pin monitoring is the important part here, as the 12V-2x6 connection carries current on six 12V pins with a rating of about 9A, with Asus’s warning at 9.2A, and exceeding the per-pin limit has led to melted connectors . An RTX 5090 is rated at 575W of board power, which is close to the connector’s 600W rating. articles.title: On this day in space! Nov. 21, 1676: Danish astronomer discovers speed of light — by accident — while observing Jupiter's moon Io
articles.summary: On Nov. 21, 1676, the Danish astronomer Ole Rømer discovered the speed of light . Before Rømer figured it out, scientists thought that light travels instantaneously, or infinitely fast. Rømer disproved this almost by accident when he was studying Jupiter's moon Io . He was trying to figure out how long it takes Io to orbit Jupiter in hopes of using it as a cosmic clock. He watched Io disappear behind Jupiter and reappear on the other side. He did this over and over every 42 hours for years. To his surprise, the timing of the eclipses was not consistent. When Earth was closest to Jupiter, the eclipses happened 11 minutes early. Likewise, when the two planets were farthest away, the eclipses were 11 minutes behind schedule. Rømer figured out the pattern and made an accurate prediction for Io's eclipse on Nov. 9, 1676. Then on Nov. 21, he took his findings to the Royal Academy of Sciences and explained that a finite speed of light must be responsible. articles.summary: The first Starship upper stage that SpaceX ever successfully recovered won't fly again. That vehicle, known as Ship 42, launched Nov. 13 on Starship 's 15th test flight. But that's not going to happen. He didn't say where Ship would be put on display, but the likeliest locale is Starbase, SpaceX's Starship manufacturing and launch hub. The STS-88 astronauts connected the two modules in orbit. Zarya was built by the Russians, but it was paid for by the United States. NASA contracted a Russian company to build it for half the price of what the American company Lockheed Martin would have charged. These days, Zarya is mainly used for storage and for external fuel tanks. The module also has docking ports for Russian Progress cargo ships and Soyuz spacecraft that carry crews to and from the space station. Today, the I nternational Space Station is about the size of a football field and typically hosts up to seven crewmembers. But back in 1998, it was a pretty tight squeeze. articles.title: Beyls: Wrapping up LLVM's relicensing effort
articles.summary: Kristof Beyls has published a summary to the LLVM discussion forum to announce that the project is declaring success and bringing its relicensing effort to a close after eight years. We've been asking past contributors to relicense their work since 2018. New contributions have come in under Apache-2.0 WITH LLVM-exception since January 19, 2019. Code contributed before that date was under LLVM's earlier licenses (UIUC/NCSA, plus MIT for some runtime libraries), so we needed permission from its authors to move it over. [...] Today, more than 99.5% of all lines of code ever contributed to LLVM are either covered by the new license, too small for copyright to apply, or no longer in the repository. Rather than trying to " chase the last tiny fraction forever " LLVM is winding up the effort. Any contributors with code contributed before January 19, 2019 who have not signed a relicensing agreement and do not want their contributions made available under Apache-2.0 with the LLVM-exception can still reach out to the project to ensure their code has the appropriate SPDX license identifier.

articles.title: Astronomers witness a star eating its companion in 1st-of-its-kind observation
articles.summary: Astronomers may have, for the first time ever, directly witnessed a star engulfing its companion, a new study reports. As stars die, they swell up to hundreds of times their original size, consuming anything orbiting nearby. In a binary star system, this can include a dying star merging with its companion star. However, scientists had never directly seen any examples of such a cosmic drama unfolding — until now. "Catching a star engulfing its companion in the act is very difficult," study lead author Viraj Karambelkar, an astrophysicist at Columbia University in New York, told Space.com. "When a star engulfs its companion, its effect is very subtle — like throwing a bucket of water in a large ocean. We need sensitive telescopes monitoring the sky for a long time in order to catch this effect." In December 2025, observations from NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope provided the final evidence that allowed researchers to fully reconstruct what happened before, during, and after the merger of a binary star system nicknamed Bao in the Andromeda galaxy.
